key_idea: A tree that is closer can hide all or part of a tree behind it.
steps: Stand at B, at the bottom left, and look toward the trees.
The top-left tree and the bottom-left tree can be seen whole.
The bottom-left tree is in front of the other 3 trees and hides part of each of them.
So from B the beaver sees exactly 2 complete trees.

choice_feedback.A: From A, the top-left tree hides the other top trees, but the 2 bottom trees can both be seen whole.
choice_feedback.C: From C, the 3 top trees can all be seen whole.
choice_feedback.D: From D, the top-right tree hides the other top trees, but the 2 bottom trees can both be seen whole.
choice_feedback.E: From E, the 2 trees on the right and the top-middle tree can be seen whole.

review.note: Figure is tight: from A the bottom-right tree only just clears the bottom-left tree, and from D the bottom-left tree only just clears the bottom-right one. If the thick outlines count as part of the trees, A and D also see exactly 2. Consider moving A and D so they clearly see 3.
